title: History & Landscape of Image Models
blurb: Tests the three eras of computer vision, what changed in 2012, the CNN era and the post-CNN split into transformers and generative models, CLIP's role in text-to-image systems, and why HOG lost to raw pixels on a small, clean dataset.

questions.prompt: In the hand-crafted era, what was trained?
options: Both the feature extractor and the classifier, end to end
Only the classifier on top of the fixed features
Nothing. Hand-crafted systems needed no training.
Only the feature extractor, with a fixed classifier
questions.explanation: A human designed the extractor, such as HOG or SIFT, and an SVM or logistic regression learned on top. End to end training came with CNNs.

refLinks.label: §67.2.1 The Three Eras of Turning Pixels Into Meaning

questions.prompt: What core insight do SIFT and HOG encode?
options: Gradients are more robust to lighting than pixels.
Pixels near the image centre carry the most information.
Colour histograms identify objects better than shapes.
Deep networks need features computed in advance.
questions.explanation: Both summarise edges and gradients, which change less than raw intensities when lighting or pose shifts.

questions.prompt: Which ingredients converged in the 2012 AlexNet moment? Select all that apply.
options: ImageNet, over a million labelled photos
ReLU activations and dropout
A transformer architecture borrowed from NLP
A deep convolutional network trained on GPUs
questions.explanation: Transformers came to vision in 2020 with ViT. AlexNet's win came from depth, GPUs, ReLU and dropout, and ImageNet's scale.

options: From GPUs to CPUs for training large models
From neural networks back to hand-crafted features
From designing features to letting training learn them from data
From labelled data to unlabelled data
questions.explanation: The field's centre of gravity moved to learned features and never moved back.

questions.prompt: What wall did very deep plain CNNs hit, and what fixed it?
options: Vanishing gradients, fixed by residuals
Slow inference, fixed by quantisation
Too few labelled images, fixed by ImageNet
Overfitting, fixed by smaller kernels
questions.explanation: Residual connections (Chapter 69) made 50 to 150+ layer networks trainable as a practical default.

questions.prompt: What does CLIP contribute to text-to-image systems?
options: A faster convolution for high-resolution images
A shared image-text embedding for prompts
The diffusion process that turns noise into images
A dataset of labelled photos for classification
questions.explanation: A CLIP-style text encoder steers a diffusion model's generation toward the prompt. Diffusion itself is the generator.

questions.prompt: Which generative approach became dominant by around 2020, per the chapter?
options: Diffusion models
Plain autoencoders
Variational autoencoders
Generative adversarial networks
questions.explanation: The lineage ran autoencoders, VAEs (2013), GANs (2014), then diffusion (2020), which took over by a wide margin.

questions.prompt: When does Procedure 67.1 lean towards classical features plus a simple classifier?
options: Small, clean data, no GPU, or a need to explain
Any time a pretrained transformer is available
Whenever accuracy matters more than cost
Large, messy, high-resolution photos with clutter
questions.explanation: Large, messy data is where learned models shine. Small, clean or interpretability-bound problems can favour classical pipelines.

questions.prompt: Which property favours hand-crafted features over learned ones, per the comparison table?
options: Robustness to messy lighting and occlusion at scale
Freedom from any design decisions
Interpretability
Accuracy on large datasets
questions.explanation: Learned features are more robust given enough data, but they're harder to interpret. Hand-crafted features are designed, so what they measure is known.

refLinks.label: §67.2.3 Classical vs. Learned Features, Side by Side

questions.prompt: What does Procedure 67.2's quick baseline do?
options: Trains a small CNN for one epoch
Logistic regression on raw pixels
Extracts HOG features and fits an SVM
Calls a managed vision API for labels
questions.explanation: It's the cheapest possible approach. If it's close to what you need, a deep model may not be worth it, and if not, it shows the headroom.

options: Setting orientations to 8 instead of 9
Assuming HOG or SIFT will beat raw pixels by default
Using HOG features with a linear classifier
Extracting HOG features from the test set too
questions.explanation: HOG's value is robustness in messy photos. On clean, small data, the gradient step can discard information. Measure, don't assume.

questions.prompt: Which approach beat both HOG pipelines on the 8×8 digits dataset?
options: HOG with logistic regression, at 0.819
None. HOG won every comparison.
HOG with an RBF-kernel SVM, at 0.861
Raw pixels with logistic regression
questions.explanation: Raw pixels scored 0.958 against 0.819 and 0.861 for HOG. The learned CNN topped all four at 0.964.

questions.prompt: The CNN scored 0.964 and raw pixels 0.958. By how many percentage points did the CNN win? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 0.964 − 0.958 = 0.006, or 0.6 points: a modest gap, not the dramatic one the 2012 story might suggest.

questions.prompt: Why did HOG do worse than raw pixels here?
options: HOG was configured wrongly and should have used larger cells.
Logistic regression can't use HOG features at all.
The digits are clean, so HOG's robustness adds nothing.
The test set was much smaller than the training set.
questions.explanation: With no lighting or pose variation, the gradient histograms throw away information instead of distilling it.

questions.prompt: What does the digits result say about the 2012 story?
options: CNNs only work on images larger than 8×8.
AlexNet's edge needed ImageNet's scale and mess.
Hand-crafted features beat learned ones on any dataset.
The 2012 story was wrong, and learned features never mattered.
questions.explanation: Learned features pull ahead where data is large and messy. The lesson isn't that classical CV is bad, but that newer isn't automatically better.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the era (hand-crafted features / learned discriminative / learned generative and multimodal) each of the following belongs to, and give one reason: (a) HOG; (b) ResNet; (c) CLIP.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) HOG: hand-crafted features era; a human-designed gradient-orientation descriptor, not learned from data. (b) ResNet: learned discriminative era; a deep CNN trained end-to-end via gradient descent for classification. (c) CLIP: learned generative and multimodal era; a jointly-trained image-text embedding model underpinning text-conditioned generation.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why the 2012 AlexNet result was a discontinuity rather than an incremental improvement, using this chapter's three converging factors.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: AlexNet was a discontinuity because it required three factors to converge simultaneously, not one incremental improvement: a large enough labelled dataset (ImageNet, 2009), enough GPU compute to train a deep network in a practical time, and architectural/training tricks (ReLU, dropout) that made deep training actually work. No single one of these existed early enough alone, so their simultaneous arrival in 2012 produced a step change rather than a gradual climb.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 67.1 as a starting point, run the raw-pixel baseline on a dataset of your choosing (or the `sklearn` digits dataset if none is available) and report the mean and standard deviation of 5-fold cross-validated accuracy.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Answer depends on the dataset actually run. Using `sklearn`'s digits dataset, expect roughly 95-97% mean 5-fold cross-validated accuracy for a raw-pixel baseline (logistic regression or SVM on flattened pixel vectors), with a standard deviation on the order of 1 percentage point given the dataset's small size and relative cleanliness.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 67.2, vary the `pixels_per_cell` parameter to `(2, 2)` and `(8, 8)` and report how HOG feature vector length and test accuracy change relative to the `(4, 4)` setting used in this chapter's Worked Example.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Smaller `pixels_per_cell` (e.g. `(2, 2)`) increases the number of cells and hence feature-vector length substantially (finer spatial resolution, more gradient bins), typically at some accuracy cost from noisier per-cell gradient estimates on this small dataset. Larger `pixels_per_cell` (e.g. `(8, 8)`) sharply reduces feature-vector length (coarser spatial pooling), which on small low-resolution digit images may lose too much spatial detail and reduce accuracy relative to the `(4, 4)` setting used in the chapter.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer wants a vision model to sort defective from non-defective parts on a production line, using cropped, well-lit, top-down camera images against a fixed background. Using Procedure 67.1, write the two or three sentences you would actually say about whether to start with a classical or learned approach.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "For cropped, well-lit, top-down images against a fixed background, this is close to the controlled-data case where classical hand-crafted features have historically been competitive or better. Worth trying a fast classical baseline (HOG + SVM/logistic regression) first before reaching for a learned model, since the constrained imaging setup doesn't need the robustness-to-messiness a CNN buys, and the classical route ships faster with less data and compute."

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter's Worked Example found HOG underperforming raw pixels. Propose one change to the dataset (not the algorithm) that the chapter's own reasoning predicts would make HOG the stronger choice, and justify it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Adding real-world messiness, varied lighting, pose, occlusion, or background clutter, to the dataset would plausibly make HOG the stronger relative choice is the wrong direction; per this chapter's own comparison table, learned features are specifically *more* robust to that kind of messiness. The change that would favor HOG instead is the opposite: an even smaller, cleaner, more tightly controlled dataset than the one used, where HOG's data efficiency advantage matters more and there isn't enough data for a learned model to find a robust pattern.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the Dalal and Triggs HOG paper cited above. Identify one design decision in the original pedestrian-detection pipeline that this chapter's simplified digit-classification pipeline omits, and explain what problem that omitted piece was solving.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. The original Dalal and Triggs pipeline includes a sliding-window multi-scale detection procedure (scanning a HOG+SVM classifier across many window positions and scales to *locate* pedestrians in a full image). This chapter's simplified digit-classification pipeline omits the sliding-window/localization step entirely, since it classifies a single pre-cropped image rather than detecting and localizing an object within a larger scene.
